Price the service call, not just the part.

Build a repair quote from diagnostic time, repair time, travel, parts markup, callback reserve, and overhead. Then see whether finishing that repair still beats recommending replace — what the customer pays per remaining year, and what you keep if they decline.

The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

Repair vs replace this machine

A $635 target on a machine with three years left can still lose to a $799 replacement that lasts ten. Distinct from a boiler winters-of-patches bid: this is one service-call quote against remaining years, plus the diagnostic you already earned if they walk.

Common questions

Why isn't the walk-away floor the same as the target price?

The walk-away floor is your modeled cost — labor, marked-up parts, trip cost, callback reserve, and overhead — with zero profit in it. The target price divides that cost by 1 − margin, so a 30% target margin on a $444.68 cost quotes $635.25, not $444.68 plus 30%. Anything you collect below the floor loses money on this job the moment you factor in the reserve and overhead you already built into it.

How does the callback / warranty reserve actually get priced in?

It's a percentage of labor, marked-up parts, and trip cost combined — not of the final price — and it lands before overhead and margin are applied, so it compounds with both rather than sitting outside them. A 5% reserve on a $385 direct job adds $19.25 to the base the overhead percentage and the margin formula then both work from, which is why a callback rate that looks small on paper still moves the quoted price by more than 5%.

If the customer declines and I recommend replace, what do I actually keep?

Whatever diagnostic or trip fee you collect for the visit, plus anything you keep from selling or installing the replacement unit — separate from the profit you'd have made finishing the repair. The calculator compares that total against your repair profit directly, so you can see in dollars whether walking with the diagnostic and a referral beats finishing the job, not just whether the customer prefers one option.

Why can the repair be the better deal for you and the worse deal for the customer at the same time?

Because the two sides are measured differently: your side compares total profit kept, the customer's side compares price per remaining year of service. A repair with a high margin can still cost a customer more per year than a replacement that lasts three times longer, even though it's the more profitable job for you to finish — which is exactly the tension the repair-vs-replace verdict is built to surface instead of hide.

Why does parts markup apply before overhead and margin, not after?

Parts markup is added once, to the parts cost itself, before that marked-up figure joins labor and trip cost as part of direct cost. Overhead and the callback reserve then apply to that combined direct cost, and target margin applies last, to the full cost including overhead — so a change to parts markup ripples through the reserve, the overhead dollar amount, and the final target price, not just the parts line.

APPLIANCE REPAIR QUOTE CALCULATOR

Should I repair or replace this appliance?

A technician on a driveway already has the quote. The harder question is whether to send it. A $635 dryer repair on a twelve-year-old machine can still be the honest number for this visit and the wrong number for the next three years.

This page does not appraise remaining life. It divides the quote you already built by the years you expect that repair to buy, then divides a replacement price by the years you expect the new machine to last. Side by side it also shows what you keep if they take the repair versus what you keep if they pay the diagnostic and walk.

The default driveway

On the calculator defaults — half an hour of diagnosis, 1.5 hours of repair, half an hour of travel, $80 loaded labor, a $35 trip, $120 of parts at 25% markup, a 5% callback reserve, 10% overhead, and a 30% target — the quote is $635.25. Three remaining years on that machine is $211.75 per year. A $799 replacement that lasts ten years is $79.90 per year. Replace is $131.85 a year cheaper for the customer.

You still keep $190.57 if they take the repair, and $75 if they pay the diagnostic and leave. The honest tension is the point: the repair still pays you more, and it still costs the customer more per remaining year.

When the repair flips back

Give the repaired unit eight years instead of three. The same $635.25 falls to $79.41 a year and undercuts the $79.90 replacement. Both books then point at finishing the repair. Sell or install the replacement for $150 and the default three-year driveway flips the other way: you keep $225 walking, and replace wins for both of you.

Open the quote calculator and change the years. The table updates from the same numbers you already typed.

What this is not

  • Not a remaining-life appraisal, a manufacturer warranty reading, or a safety inspection.
  • Not the same decision as a boiler winters-of-patches bid. That tool prices repeated call-backs against replacing the plant. This one prices a single service call.
  • Not advice to sell a replacement or to finish a repair. The rates are inputs.

Common questions

Should I repair or replace this appliance?

On the calculator defaults a $635.25 repair target on a machine expected to last three more years costs $211.75 per remaining year. A $799 replacement expected to last ten years costs $79.90 per year. Replace is $131.85 a year cheaper for the customer. Finishing the repair still leaves the technician $115.57 more than walking with a $75 diagnostic. Those are planning figures from the rates you type, not a recommendation.

When does the repair still beat replace?

If the repaired unit is expected to last eight years, the same $635.25 quote falls to $79.41 per year and undercuts the $79.90 replacement. The repair then beats replace for both the customer and the technician's book.

What if I sell or install the replacement?

Add what you keep on that replacement. At $150, walking with the $75 diagnostic plus the replacement leaves $225, which beats the $190.57 repair profit. Recommend replace on those numbers.

Is this the same as a boiler repair-versus-replace bid?

No. A boiler bid prices winters of patch calls against replacing the plant. This page prices one appliance service-call quote against remaining years on that machine.

vs-a-flat-rate-repair-price.html.text:
← Appliance Repair Quote Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat rate repair price

“Refrigerator not cooling, $635, done” is not a price for a repair — it is a price for one guess at what is actually wrong, quietly applied to every call that starts with the same complaint.

What a flat rate repair price is

A flat rate repair price comes from a price book: a fixed dollar figure per job category, looked up by the customer's complaint and quoted before the unit is opened up. It is fast to quote over the phone, and it is the number a customer holding a competitor's flat rate will ask you to match.

The number behind each category was set once, usually from the most common version of that complaint — a simple part with a short repair — and then reused for every call in that category, whether the actual fault turns out to be the common one or a much bigger job hiding behind the same symptom.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter your diagnostic, repair, and travel hours, your loaded labor rate, trip cost, parts cost and your own markup on it, a callback or warranty reserve, your overhead rate, and your target margin. It prices the labor, the marked-up parts, and the reserve as their own lines and returns the walk-away price, the target-margin quote, and your effective hourly rate — for this call, not a book price for every call under the same complaint.

What a flat rate repair price doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same figure for every call filed under one complaint, whether the fault turns out to be a $10 part or a $450 sealed-system component. Prices parts at your own cost with your own markup applied, so a call that turns up an expensive part costs more than one that does not — on this call, not the category average.
Has one labor figure baked into the category price, with no separate line for a repair that runs longer than the common case. Prices diagnostic, repair, and travel hours separately at your loaded rate, so a longer repair is priced for the hours it actually takes.
Has no line for a callback or warranty reserve — if the fix does not hold, that cost comes out of the same flat number. Adds a callback/warranty reserve as its own percentage of direct cost, so a repeat visit is already funded rather than eating the job's margin.
Bakes an assumed overhead into the category price rather than your shop's own rate. Applies your own overhead rate to the direct cost, so the price reflects your burden, not an averaged one.
Gives the technician a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the effective hourly rate, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you say a number at the door.

Two “not cooling” calls, one flat price

Using this calculator's own shipped starting example:

A simple repair — 0.5 diagnostic hours, 1.5 repair hours, 0.5 travel hours, and a $120 part — costs $444.68 to run and this calculator prices it at $635.25 at a 30% target margin.

Take the same complaint and make it the harder version instead — a sealed-system repair that takes 3.5 repair hours and a $450 part instead of 1.5 hours and $120, everything else unchanged — and the call costs $1,105.91 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices it at $1,579.88: 2.49 times the easy call's price, filed under the identical complaint. Quoting the hard call at the easy call's flat $635.25 price prices it $470.66 below its own break-even cost — before counting the $944.63 it falls short of this calculator's own price at the same 30% target margin. Same complaint, same flat price, one call that pays and one that loses money the moment the sealed system shows up.

Common questions

Why does a flat rate repair price get an appliance repair wrong?

Because a flat rate price book prices the complaint, not the repair. "Refrigerator not cooling" is one line in the book with one price attached, whether the actual fault is a $10 evaporator fan that swaps in under an hour or a sealed-system compressor that needs recovery, brazing, a new drier, recharge, and half a day. Two calls that sound identical on the phone can carry completely different parts cost and repair hours once the tech is actually inside the unit, and a price set from the symptom alone cannot tell them apart.

What does a flat rate repair price usually leave out entirely?

Your own labor rate, your parts markup, a callback or warranty reserve, and overhead. A price-book rate is usually set once, off an averaged or vendor-supplied job, and then quoted for every call in that category regardless of what your diagnostic actually finds, what you pay for the part that day, or what your shop's real burden and overhead run. It has no line that moves when the repair turns out bigger than the category suggested.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped starting example: a simple repair -- 0.5 diagnostic hours, 1.5 repair hours, 0.5 travel hours, and a $120 part -- costs $444.68 to run and prices at $635.25 at a 30% target margin. A harder repair under the same "not cooling" complaint -- 3.5 repair hours and a $450 sealed-system part, everything else unchanged -- costs $1,105.91 to run and this calculator prices it at $1,579.88, 2.49 times the easy call's price. Quoting the hard call at the easy call's flat $635.25 price prices it $470.66 below its own break-even cost, before counting the $944.63 it falls short of this calculator's own price at the same 30% target margin. Same complaint, same flat price, one call that pays and one that loses money the moment the sealed system shows up.

Is a flat rate repair price ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow, genuinely common repair -- the same part, the same access, the same hours, most times you see that complaint -- a flat rate number can land close, because that is probably the job the price was averaged from. The risk is the call that turns out to be the harder version of the same symptom, because the price does not know which one it is until the panel is off, and by then the flat number has often already been quoted at the door.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or parts costs?

No. It has no price book and no data on your local labor market or parts supplier pricing. It takes your diagnostic, repair, and travel hours, your loaded labor rate, trip cost, parts cost and your own markup on it, a callback/warranty reserve, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into a price for this call -- the arithmetic a flat rate price skips, not a market survey.

Open the Appliance Repair Quote Calculator to price your own call, or read Should I repair or replace this appliance?

No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, financial, engineering, or business advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. Verify every figure against your own payroll, insurance, supplier invoices, and site conditions, and against a qualified professional, before relying on it or quoting a customer. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device, and this page makes no live comparison against any competing service — it is a static page describing the calculator's own worked example.

This calculator vs. Housecall Pro

Two different shapes: Housecall Pro runs a home-service business — scheduling, dispatch, invoicing, payments. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this repair cost, and does finishing it still beat telling the customer to replace.

What each tool is for

Housecall Pro is field service management software for home service businesses, used as a central hub for the work around a job rather than the pricing of one. It covers a drag-and-drop scheduling calendar, real-time dispatch, automated on-my-way texts with GPS tracking, online booking, recurring service plans, a mobile app that lets a technician pull up the work order and record repair notes without returning to the office, estimates and invoicing with automated payment reminders, card payments, and a QuickBooks integration. It is sold as an ongoing account for the business, and it publishes that it is used by over 200,000 field service professionals across HVAC, plumbing, electrical, cleaning, and other trades. Housecall Pro's current plan names and dollar figures are not verified from this page, so none are repeated here: only its well-documented identity and category — field service management software, sold as an ongoing account — are stated, and no price for Housecall Pro appears anywhere on this page.

This calculator does none of what Housecall Pro does. It does not schedule a job, dispatch a van, send an invoice, or take a payment, and it holds no customer record between visits. It takes one service call — diagnostic and labor hours at your loaded rate, parts at cost with your markup applied to the parts themselves before anything else, trip cost, a callback and warranty reserve charged as a percentage of that combined direct cost, overhead, and target margin — and turns that into the walk-away floor below which the job loses money, the target-margin quote, the effective hourly rate you actually earn, and a repair-versus-replace verdict measured from both sides at once: the customer's price per remaining year of service, and what you keep if they decline and you sell the replacement instead. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I need today's calls scheduled, my techs dispatched, and the customer texted when someone is on the way.Housecall Pro, or a comparable field service platform — running the business day is not something this calculator does.
Does this quote actually clear my cost, once parts markup, trip cost, callback reserve and overhead have all compounded?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
The customer is asking whether to fix it or replace it. Which answer is honest, and which one pays me better?This calculator's repair-versus-replace verdict, which reports both and says plainly when they disagree.
I need invoices sent, reminders chased, and cards charged without me doing it by hand.Housecall Pro — built as an ongoing account for exactly that.
What is the lowest number I can say at the door without losing money on this job?This calculator's walk-away floor.
How should I think about repair versus replace before I quote it?This calculator's own repair-or-replace walkthrough.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. Housecall Pro is used through an ongoing account.

Most independent technicians get different value from each: a field service platform for scheduling, dispatch, invoicing and payments as an ongoing account, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login check on whether one repair's price clears cost and margin before the number is said out loud. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a work order, an invoice, or a remaining-life appraisal.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Housecall Pro?

They do different jobs, and most working technicians end up wanting both. Housecall Pro is field service management software for home service businesses: a drag-and-drop scheduling calendar, real-time dispatch, automated on-my-way texts with GPS tracking, online booking, recurring service plans, a mobile app that lets a tech view the work order and record repair notes in the field, estimates and invoicing with automated reminders, card payments, and a QuickBooks integration. It is sold as an ongoing account for running the business, and it says it is used by over 200,000 field service professionals across HVAC, plumbing, electrical, cleaning and other trades. This calculator does none of that. It takes one service call — diagnostic and labor hours at your loaded rate, parts at your cost with your markup applied before anything else, trip cost, a callback and warranty reserve as a percentage of that direct cost, overhead, and target margin — and turns it into the walk-away floor below which the job loses money, the target-margin quote, the effective hourly rate you actually earn, and a repair-versus-replace verdict measured two ways at once: the customer's cost per remaining year, and what you keep if they decline. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A shop dispatching techs, booking jobs and chasing invoices across every customer is better served by Housecall Pro or a comparable platform; a technician who wants an instant, private check on whether one quote clears cost and margin before saying a number out loud is in the right place here.

Does Housecall Pro price an appliance repair for me?

Field service platforms are built to move a job through scheduling, dispatch, invoicing and payment, and they hold whatever price book or flat-rate pricing you put into them. What they do not do is derive that number from your own cost structure for one specific repair. Reviewers also note that appliance repair contractors get comparatively little trade-specific tooling in Housecall Pro next to HVAC and plumbing, where equipment tracking and service-plan features are more developed. This calculator is the step before the price book: it works out what a repair actually costs you once parts markup, trip cost, callback reserve and overhead compound, so the number you load into a platform — or say at the door — has a floor under it.
